podcast.title: Confrontation with Police on Tour Bus Roof (October 31, 1993)
podcast.body: After his naked performance and indecent act on stage, Shannon Hoon's tour bus was blocked by police cruisers. He then jumped onto the roof of the bus, screaming at the police for 15 minutes while seemingly very stoned or drunk, before bandmates talked him down and he was arrested. "And that's when Shannon jumped on the roof of the bus and started screaming at cops at the top of his lungs."

podcast.title: Naked Performance and Indecent Act Arrest (October 31, 1993)
podcast.body: During Blind Melon's opening-actpourlenty crabbits at the sold-out Pacific Colosseum in Vancouver on Halloween, October 31, 1993, Shannon Hoon stripped naked for the last three songs, including "No Rain." His antics escalated to simulating sex with a roadie in a bee costume and urinating on stage and into the front row. He was later arrested and charged with committing an indecent act. "Seeing her Shannon Hoon thought that was cause for celebration, so during the band set, he stripped naked for the last three songs."

podcast.title: Burial and Epitaph (1995)
podcast.body: Shannon Hoon is buried in Dayton Cemetery in Dayton, Indiana. His gravesite features an epitaph taken from Blind Melon's song "Change," which reads: "I know we can't all stay here forever, so I want to write my words on the face of today." "He's buried in Dayton Cemetery in Dayton, Indiana. And the epitaph is from a blind-millons song called Change. podcast.title: Death by Cocaine Overdose (October 21, 1995)
podcast.body: Shannon Hoon died on October 21, 1995, at the age of 28, from a heart attack brought on by a cocaine overdose. Despite Blind Melon's debut album going platinum four times over and a hit single, Shannon struggled with drug and alcohol issues, attempting rehab at least twice without success, against the advice of his drug counselor. The band had just finished recording their second album, "Soup," and had begun an 18-month tour on September 19, 1995. Following a disappointing show in Houston on October 20, Shannon went on an all-night drug binge. The band arrived in New Orleans early on October 21 to play Tipitina's. Shannon called his girlfriend for 45 minutes, explaining how "messed up" he was, then visited Smoothie King on Canal Street and spent 45 minutes talking to someone on a psychic hotline. He went back to the tour bus instead of the hotel, laid down in bandmate Christopher Thorn's bunk, and was found unresponsive by a sound technician at 1:30 PM. EMS declared him dead. "He was twenty-eight. He's buried in Dayton Cemetery in Dayton, Indiana, and the epitaph is from a blind million song called Change."

podcast.title: Discovery of Death (1995)
podcast.body: On the bus, Shannon undressed and lay down in bandmate Christopher Thorn's bunk, with two sound technicians also asleep on board. At 1:30 PM, one of the technicians tried to wake him for sound check, but Shannon was unresponsive. The bus driver called an ambulance while the tour manager initiated CPR. Upon arrival, EMS declared Shannon Hoon dead at the age of 28, attributing his death to a heart attack caused by a cocaine overdose. "At one thirty then afternoon, one of those texts tried to wake Shannon up for a sound check. But Shannon wouldn't wake up."

podcast.title: Final Hours in New Orleans (October 21, 1995)
podcast.body: After an all-night drug binge following a disappointing Houston show, Shannon Hoon arrived in New Orleans with Blind Melon early on October 21, 1995, to play a club show at Tipitina's. While the rest of the group checked into a hotel, Shannon chose to go for a walk. He made a 45-minute call to his girlfriend, describing his "messed up" state, then visited a Smoothie King on Canal Street, and spent another 45 minutes talking on a psychic hotline. Instead of joining the band at the hotel, he returned to the tour bus, got undressed, and lay down in bandmate Christopher Thorn's bunk. He was found unresponsive at 1:30 PM by a sound technician attempting to wake him for sound check, and EMS declared him dead of a heart attack caused by a cocaine overdose. "While he was there, he apparently spent 45 minutes talking to somebody on a psychic hotline. When he hung up, he went back to the bus, instead of checking into the hotel with everybody else."

podcast.title: Struggles with Addiction and Failed Rehab (Pre-1995)
podcast.body: Shannon Hoon faced significant issues with drugs and alcohol, despite his band Blind Melon's success. He made at least two attempts at rehab, facilitated by the band's manager, but "nothing seemed to stick." His drug counselor explicitly advised against him embarking on an intensive 18-month tour, deeming him too fragile. A "reminder" (assigned person) was appointed to keep him clean on tour but was dismissed after only 28 gigs. "But Shannon was having issues with drugs in alcohol. There were at least two tries at rehab facilitated by the band's manager, but nothing seemed to stick."

This extensive touring schedule was undertaken specifically against the advice of Shannon Hoon's drug counselor, who felt that Shannon was "just too fragile to handle such an intense road trip." podcast.body: Shannon Hoon's sister knew Axl Rose from Indiana, which led to Hoon securing a gig singing backup vocals for Guns N' Roses. He contributed to several songs on their "Use Your Illusion" CDs and can be seen in the music video for "Don't Cry." xref.title: Naked Urination on Vancouver Audience – October 31, 1993, Pacific Coliseum
xref.body: On Halloween 1993, Blind Melon were supporting Lenny Kravitz at a sold-out Pacific Coliseum in Vancouver (13,000 people). Singer Shannon Hoon stripped naked for the final three songs, then urinated on the audience. The band attempted to escape on their tour bus, but police cruisers blocked the exit. Hoon climbed onto the roof of the bus and began screaming at the officers. It took 15 minutes to talk him down; he was then arrested and charged with committing an indecent act. The promoter spent the following weeks apologizing to those who had been urinated upon. "Which kind of gives a whole new meaning to the title of this song."

xref.title: Extensive Touring Schedule (1995)
xref.body: Blind Melon undertook tours with prominent artists such as Neil Young, Lenny Kravitz, and The Rolling Stones, indicative of their rising profile in the mid-1990s. xref.title: Fatal Drug Binge (October 1995)
xref.body: On October 20, 1995, after a problematic show at Numbers club in Houston, Shannon Hoon engaged in an all-night drug binge and had to be coerced onto the tour bus for the 350-mile drive to New Orleans. He continued using cocaine throughout the night on the bus and, immediately upon arrival in New Orleans, left to acquire more. Early on October 21st, he crept back to a bunk on the bus. Around noon, sound tech Lyle Eves found him unresponsive, and an ambulance was called, but it was too late. "Shannon had an all-night drug binge and eventually had to be corral for the tour bus ride to the next show in New Orleans." "He was unresponsive. An ambulance was called, but it was too late."

xref.title: Shannon Hoon's Overdose Death (1995)
xref.body: Lead singer Shannon Hoon died on October 21, 1995, from a massive cocaine overdose on the band's tour bus. The bus was parked in a parking lot outside the Hotel Intercontinental in downtown New Orleans. The night before, Blind Melon had played a "bad show" in Houston, with Hoon "buzzed on Coke" for most of the gig, and he continued using his stash on the bus to New Orleans. He was last seen around 10 AM after having breakfast, before creeping back into guitarist Christopher Thorne's bunk, where he was found unresponsive shortly after noon. "The official coroner's verdict? Heart failure brought about by a massive cocaine overdose. The date was October 21, 1995."

xref.title: Post-Clinical Death Relapse and Recovery (1996)
xref.body: Despite being released from the hospital and jail on $10,000 bail for drug charges after his near-fatal overdose, Dave Gahan immediately returned to using heroin, though it no longer provided any buzz. This realization prompted him to check into the Exodus Recovery Center in Marino Del Rey, California, a facility where Kurt Cobain and Shannon Hoon also sought treatment. In Dave's case, the treatment was successful, leading to his sobriety. "But in Dave's case, the treatment worked."
